chief_complaint: severe neck pain radiating to jaw and fever after viral infection
hpi_details: 35F with painful, exquisite anterior neck tenderness, low-grade fever, and transient thyrotoxicosis 3 weeks post-URI. High ESR, low RAIU.
ideas: She thinks the severe pain in the front of her neck and jaw is an aggressive throat infection or an infected lymph node left over from her recent cold.
concerns: She is worried that the severe throat and jaw pain will make it impossible to swallow food or speak at her full-time job.
expectations: She hopes to get strong anti-inflammatory pain medication and antibiotics to quickly knock out whatever is infecting her throat.

clinical_knowledge.topic: De Quervain (Subacute) Thyroiditis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of De Quervain (Subacute) Thyroiditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes treating thyroid pain with NSAIDs or glucocorticoids and controlling thyrotoxic symptoms with a beta-blocker, while avoiding antithyroid drugs since hormone release is from destructive thyroiditis rather than overproduction, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe neck pain radiating to jaw and fever after viral infection
Key HPI features: 35F with painful, exquisite anterior neck tenderness, low-grade fever, and transient thyrotoxicosis 3 weeks post-URI. High ESR, low RAIU.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for De Quervain Subacute Thyroiditis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out De Quervain (Subacute) Thyroiditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Graves' disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever with severe systemic toxicity — would suggest bacterial thyroiditis instead.
management_principles: Treat thyroid pain and inflammation with an NSAID or, if severe or unresponsive, glucocorticoids; use a beta-blocker for thyrotoxic symptoms, but do not use antithyroid drugs because hormone release is from destructive thyroiditis
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of De Quervain Subacute Thyroiditis: severe neck pain radiating to jaw and fever after viral infection. 35F with painful, exquisite anterior neck tenderness, low-grade fever, and transient thyrotoxicosis 3 weeks post-URI. High ESR, low RAIU.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for De Quervain Subacute Thyroiditis.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of De Quervain Subacute Thyroiditis.
reference_soap.plan: Treat pain and inflammation with an NSAID; use glucocorticoids if pain is severe or does not respond. Use a beta-blocker for troublesome palpitations or tremor. Do not prescribe antithyroid drugs because the transient thyrotoxicosis is due to release of preformed hormone. Monitor thyroid function for a hypothyroid phase and recovery.

teaching.one_liner: A viral-triggered inflammation of the thyroid causing exquisite neck tenderness and transient thyrotoxicosis weeks after a respiratory infection — self-limited, distinguished from Graves' by a low radioactive iodine uptake.
red_flags: High fever with severe systemic toxicity — would suggest bacterial thyroiditis instead

must_ask.say: Is your neck very tender to touch, and does the pain move to your jaw or ear?
Did you have a cold or viral infection a few weeks ago?
Have you felt your heart racing or unusually anxious?
How long has the neck pain lasted?

history.answer: Doctor, the front of my lower neck hurts terribly, and I have been running a fever.
The severe pain in my neck began about 4 days ago and has gotten progressively worse.
It is an intense, throbbing ache that rates an 8 out of 10 across the front of my throat.
Yes, the sharp pain shoots right up into my jaw and ears, especially when I turn my neck.
Swallowing hurts a lot, but I can still swallow liquids and I am definitely not drooling.
My breathing is completely clear without any wheezing or harsh sounds, and my voice sounds normal.
No, I can open my mouth all the way without any stiffness or spasm.
I have had a low-grade fever around 37.8 degrees Celsius and mild chills for the last 3 days.
About 3 weeks ago, I had a nasty cold with a runny nose, mild sore throat, and cough that cleared up after a week.
No, the cough and runny nose are completely gone now, and my eyes are not red.
The lower front of my neck feels swollen and so sore that even my shirt collar hurts to touch.
No, I have not seen any skin rashes or rough sandpaper-like spots anywhere.
I feel unusually exhausted and fatigued, but I do not have any pain in the left side of my belly.
A couple of coworkers caught the common cold when I was sick, but nobody had this severe neck pain.
I almost never get sore throats or tonsil trouble, maybe just once a year with a standard winter cold.
No, I do not suffer from heartburn, acid reflux, throat clearing, or a feeling of something stuck in my throat.
Over the past few days, I have noticed my heart pounding fast, feeling sweaty and overheated, and my hands shaking slightly.
I noticed my clothes feel slightly looser, and the scale shows I lost about 1 to 2 kilograms over the past 2 weeks.
I have been in a committed, monogamous marriage with my husband for 8 years, and I have had no new partners.
I have chronic hypertension and mild high cholesterol, but no other medical problems.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy in my early twenties, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 mg daily for blood pressure, and I took over-the-counter ibuprofen yesterday, which barely helped the pain.
I have no known drug allergies, and I have taken penicillin in the past without any reaction.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes in my life.
I only have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I work full-time as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my husband.
My mother has high blood pressure, but no one in my family has thyroid disease or hormonal issues.
My last period started 2 weeks ago, my monthly cycles are regular, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.
I thought maybe my recent cold turned into a deep throat infection or a bad swollen lymph node that spread up to my jaw.

I'm so worried because it hurts terribly whenever I swallow or turn my head, and I'm afraid I won't be able to talk or work. I'm really hoping for strong prescription pain relief and an antibiotic so I can finally swallow without agonizing pain.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 98 bpm regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 37.8 C, SpO2 99% on room air.
Alert, mildly uncomfortable female holding her neck, warm and mildly diaphoretic.
Oropharynx is clear without tonsillar enlargement, exudates, uvular deviation, or soft palate swelling.
No significant cervical lymphadenopathy palpable in the anterior or posterior cervical chains.
Thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged, firm, and exquisitely tender to gentle palpation.
Warm, smooth skin without scarlatiniform rash, petechiae, or other cutaneous lesions.
Abdomen is soft with no splenomegaly or hepatomegaly palpable.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Fine postural tremor visible in bilateral outstretched hands.
